articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting community members to share their thoughts on a proposed structure and pricing model for use of the new community pool. Residents can provide input by speaking at a Pool Advisory Committee study session tomorrow, Thursday, February 13, at 6:00 p.m. at City Hall. Community members unable to attend the meeting can submit comments by email to cputzer@ piedmont.ca.gov. Email comments received by 4pm on February 13 will be shared with Committee members at the study session. The proposed model, called “Build a Pass,” is designed to offer community members broad flexibility to purchase annual or seasonal (summer) passes that meet the unique needs of their household. In contrast to the limited pass options available at the old pool, this framework creates opportunities for everyone to access passholder benefits without paying for features they don’t need. Proposed options and pricing The model begins with a choice of base category (adult, senior, family, student), then offers add-on options (adult, senior, youth, guest) that can be mixed and matched as-needed. Visitors could choose from an annual pass, which offers the largest discount, a seasonal summer (4 month) pass, or drop-in day passes. The proposed rates are benchmarked to adult pass pricing for 2019, the last full year of pool service. Proposed pass rates would begin at 15% above 2019 levels, with annual adjustments based on inflation. Across all pass options, non-resident rates are proposed at 20% above resident pricing. Other considerations and next steps The Committee will also discuss additional benefits being considered for passholders, including: • priority access to pool use during peak hours or days (all passholders) • priority registration for swim lessons, summer swim camps, and junior lifeguarding (annual passholders) • priority reservations for Poolside Room and Pavilion rentals (annual passholders)

articles.text: The Wildwood Dads Club hosted its 38th annual Crab Feed on Saturday, February 8, at the Veterans Hall in an energetic celebration. articles.text: Editor: Piedmonters should take a good look at the depiction of housing the city is proposing be built under the Objective Design Standards (https://piedmont.ca.gov/news/objective_ design_standards_open_house_ feb_2025). That figure shows 4 units – two wall-to-wall duplexes on a lot divided 60/40 under SB9 – and is applicable to every single-family residence in Piedmont. This is a “Wistaria Way” accident waiting to happen to many residents in Piedmont. State law allows developers to build this 4-unit scenario with only 30 days of staff review and no public notice. Residents should participate in these ODS public meetings. Start by watching the YouTube video at the link. There’s an interesting semantic exercise wherein a subjective definition for front entry way is redefined in objective terms. Perhaps staff can develop objective definitions for massing, parking requirements, view, noise and yard setbacks so we can maintain the neighborhood character and privacy that Piedmonters enjoy. The Planning Department should use ODS development to preserve existing design guidelines, as best it can. -Garrett Keating 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Tony Simons Sophie Hess, Intern Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Jay Russell SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Climate Fellow Andrew Kaplowitz offers ideas for New Year’s resolutions Happy New Year! Each January, the turning of the calendar offers a reset - an opportunity to embrace new lifestyle choices. But for many of us, when the month draws to a close our most ambitious resolutions have already fallen by the wayside. Today, I offer four suggestions for simple yet impactful alternatives – planet-friendly lifestyle adjustments you can start working into your routine at any time. • Buy local Buying local can have two meanings. The first is centered on purchasing locally sourced goods - like gathering supplies at a farmer’s market or craft fair. The second is the support of small or community-based organizations. Shopping at these businesses strengthens community rapport, solidifies jobs, and improves the local economy. Buying local lowers transportation emissions that would come from traveling longer distances for goods or from services for online purchases. • Drive less As of 2022, 46% of Piedmont’s total greenhouse gas emissions came from passenger vehicles. One easy way to cut back on emissions is carpooling. Team up with a group of neighbors to rotate school drop-off trips in the morning. Fewer cars on the road means lower emissions, less congestion, and saves money on gas. There are also significant social benefits to carpooling that can foster new friendships for kids and parents alike. Alternatively, try mixing up your routine by walking, biking, or taking public transportation occasionally instead of driving. • Purchase second-hand goods Instead of ordering a new book online, browse used bookstores or the library. Instead of purchasing fast-fashion, look for vintage, upcycled, or thrifted clothes. Like shopping local, buying second-hand lowers transportation emissions. Shopping second-hand also eliminates emissions and resources used in manufacturing and packaging. • Be water conscious The simple act of turning the faucet off while brushing your teeth can save 3.75 gallons of water. Shorter showers and fewer dishwasher cycles are other easy Piedmont Climate Fellow Andrew Kaplowitz ways to conserve water at home. To calculate your water use, refer to the East Bay MUD Watersmart Calculator at https://www.ebmud. com/water/conservation-and-rebates/residential/watersmart-calculator. Bonus: being water conscious is more than just a sustainable practice – it also lowers monthly utility bills! The beauty of these resolutions is they can be attempted at any time. Even if you find yourself being inconsistent, each step you take is progress toward a sustainable future. articles.text: Construction is scheduled to begin on Friday, February 14 on a project to replace the pedestrian footbridge over Bushy Dell Creek in lower Piedmont Park. There will be path closures and detours in Piedmont Park for 4-6 weeks while the project is underway. This project, supported by State of California Proposition 68 grant funds, will replace the existing bridge with a long-term durable bridge in the same alignment, composed of a weathered steel frame with pressure-treated wood decking. A new bridge has been fabricated off-site and will be delivered to the park then installed by a crane. New footings are being constructed in advance which requires the area around the bridge. Three benches near the base of Bushy Dell Creek will be removed temporarily in order to allow truck access and will be re-installed once construction is complete. The bridge, located in the southwest portion of Piedmont Park near the PUSD softball field, was first identified as in need of replacement in 2015. The bridge is over 30 years old and has required substantial repairs twice in the past five years. Holes in the wood decking have been temporarily patched with plywood, and temporary side rails were constructed in 2023 after the original protective railings collapsed due to rotten wood. The City asks residents to respect detour signs and avoid closed paths when visiting the park.

Dear PUSD Families & Staff: At last week’s Board Study Session, the Board provided direction to staff to pursue a number of program options to implement for the fall, including additional performing arts in grades 4 and 5, additional world language in grades 5-7, and additional courses at the high school level, including AP Seminar and Vocal Music. Staff are now collaborating on what the implementation looks like. Slide deck for the budget study session: Docs.google.com/ presentation/d/1AyPbjn_DPjmkoVmBWjuK3MowvjsNSNk0cIm3aj-P8eg/edit . If you have thoughts on these options, we sent out a survey several weeks ago where you can still submit ideas, via Docs.google.com/forms/d/e/ 1FAIpQLScsmlpVTbJyLxCXlFV6Y1TJTYm1ARWmaPiPf HmYHvIbs7dTOg/viewform. Following collaboration and input from staff and families, we will present information to the Board in the months to follow. Thank you for your partnership in supporting our students. In Community, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent Once Upon a Mattress One of the many outstanding aspects of our district is our performing arts programs, including use of the Alan Harvey Theater. Congratulations to Amy Moorhead and our students for a fun production of Once Upon a Mattress, the comedic adaptation of The Princess and the Pea. As always our students were wonderful, with an array of costumes, and an enjoyable evening for all ages. Students from Spain arrive It was great to attend a reception on February 2 for students and staff from Spain (Galicia) who are part of a cultural exchange program for our high school students. Thanks to Deysi Sahagon, Ken Brown, Joanne Guillen along with parent supporters who have made this wonderful exchange program happen. Our Spanish visitors will be here through February 11, and our students and staff will visit Spain over spring vacation. Art, Literature Thanks so much to the Beach staff, including Ms. Harris for letting a Board member and me drop into her K art class where kids were creating art based on Sendak’s Where the Wild Things Are–wonderful! Later in the week, I visited high school English classes, including Dr. Marks’ AP Literature class where students were studying Milton, and Mr. Wolbert’s 9th grade English class where students were working on their I-Search projects. Many of you know I taught high school English for many years, and visiting our expert teachers amazing work! Students learn the power of words I happened upon a lesson at Havens last week in which our students were learning about the power of language, including the meaning and impact of racial slurs and discriminatory language. Thanks to Jean Takazawa for her leadership, along with our high school Affinity Mentors who facilitated the lesson for our elementary students. Thanks also to our Havens teachers for their collaboration on teaching students the importance of appropriate language and behavior. Threat Management Team - Committee members needed Pa rent s/Gu a rd ia ns: We launched a committee last year to establish safety procedures for threats to the campus. Since the launch, we have collaborated with PPD, PFD, and our staff on developing a process for threats that we hope we never need. At this point, we have a draft document that we would like to refine and finalize. We are looking for 1-2 experts in mental health threat assessment who would be willing to join our committee and advise on our internal procedures. By Jennifer Hawn Dear PUSD Families & Staff: At last week’s Board Study Session, the Board provided direction to staff to pursue a number of program options to implement for the fall, including additional performing arts in grades 4 and 5, additional world language in grades 5-7, and additional courses at the high school level, including AP Seminar and Vocal Music. Staff are now collaborating on what the implementation looks like. Slide deck for the budget study session: Docs.google.com/ presentation/d/1AyPbjn_DPjmkoVmBWjuK3MowvjsNSNk0cIm3aj-P8eg/edit . If you have thoughts on these options, we sent out a survey several weeks ago where you can still submit ideas, via Docs.google.com/forms/d/e/ 1FAIpQLScsmlpVTbJyLxCXlFV6Y1TJTYm1ARWmaPiPf HmYHvIbs7dTOg/viewform. Following collaboration and input from staff and families, we will present information to the Board in the months to follow. Thank you for your partnership in supporting our students. In Community, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent Once Upon a Mattress One of the many outstanding aspects of our district is our performing arts programs, including use of the Alan Harvey Theater. Congratulations to Amy Moorhead and our students for a fun production of Once Upon a Mattress, the comedic adaptation of The Princess and the Pea. As always our students were wonderful, with an array of costumes, and an enjoyable evening for all ages. Students from Spain arrive It was great to attend a reception on February 2 for students and staff from Spain (Galicia) who are part of a cultural exchange program for our high school students. Thanks to Deysi Sahagon, Ken Brown, Joanne Guillen along with parent supporters who have made this wonderful exchange program happen. Our Spanish visitors will be here through February 11, and our students and staff will visit Spain over spring vacation. Art, Literature Thanks so much to the Beach staff, including Ms. Harris for letting a Board member and me drop into her K art class where kids were creating art based on Sendak’s Where the Wild Things Are–wonderful! Later in the week, I visited high school English classes, including Dr. Marks’ AP Literature class where students were studying Milton, and Mr. Wolbert’s 9th grade English class where students were working on their I-Search projects. Many of you know I taught high school English for many years, and visiting our expert teachers does make me long to teach again. Thank you, teachers, for your amazing work! Students learn the power of words I happened upon a lesson at Havens last week in which our students were learning about the power of language, including the meaning and impact of racial slurs and discriminatory language. Thanks to Jean Takazawa for her leadership, along with our high school Affinity Mentors who facilitated the lesson for our elementary students. Thanks also to our Havens teachers for their collaboration on teaching students the importance of appropriate language and behavior. We are looking for 1-2 experts in mental health threat assessment who would be willing to join our committee and advise on our internal procedures. articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School (PMS) Parents Club is now selling tickets for a PMS fundraiser on Thursday, March 27, “Kickin’ It Old Skool.” This is the school’s biggest fundraiser and will take place at Piedmont Community Hall from 7:00-10:00 p.m. Party-goers will eat, drink, and dance the night away to favorite music from the 80’s and 90’s. The Kickin’ it Old Skool event, formerly known as “March Mingle,” will feature a live auction with special items including a Lake Tahoe vacation rental, a sunset cruise catered by Trader Vic’s, and sporting event tickets. Old school sneakers like Vans and Keds are recommended. There will also be a raffle and surprises that can be described as “totally radical.” Don’t miss the rare opportunity to relive memories of junior high school days and the culture unique to the era. As a bonus, the good vibes promise to keep rolling after the main event with several Parent Parties, including a Pub Quiz night and Intro to Poker. This event is crucial to raising the funds to keep them going.” Funds will support: • Counselor/Mental Health resources and events • Lunch Clubs • After School Tutoring • DEI Programming (Diversity Day, movies in celebration of culture each month) • Library Subscriptions • Emergency Preparedness Supplies • 6th Grade Welcome Programs (including Scots Camp) The PMS Fundraiser team is seeking out a few more Parent Sponsors. Please see Pef. schoolauction.net/marchmingle2025/homepages/show for more details. Parents are encouraged to attend while dressed as they did in their middle school days.

articles.text: Why it matters even in difficult times In life’s toughest moments, joy can feel out of reach. Yet creative expression—through art, music, writing, and more—often brings light to even the darkest places. Why does creating spark joy, and why is that joy essential when Creative expression connects us to something deeper. The process itself, not just the outcome, is 1. Flow State: Creative activities induce a sense of flow—a state where you become deeply absorbed, losing track of time and gaining a sense of fulfillment. 2. Emotional Release: Art externalizes feelings we can’t always verbalize, offering relief and clarity. 3. Playfulness: Creativity encourages experimentation and discovery, reigniting childlike curiosity and wonder. 4. Sense of Accomplishment: Completing a creative project, whether big or small, can spark pride and satisfaction Why joy matters during hardships Joy doesn’t erase pain but provides balance, resilience, and hope when we need it most: 1. Emotional Strength: Positive emotions replenish mental and emotional reserves, making challenges feel less overwhelming. 2. Hope and Optimism: Small moments of joy remind us that beauty and possibility coexist with hardship. 3. Connection: Sharing creativity fosters human connection—whether through community performances, collaborative projects, or heartfelt creations gifted to others. All kinds of creativity, including taking an art class, helps to spark joy in one’s life.
articles.title: Finding joy through creativity

articles.text: Fairyland’s new 75th Anniversary sign was Installed on January 28. Children’s Fairyland, America’s first storybook theme park, is celebrating its 75th anniversary in 2025. Leading up to the park’s official anniversary on Tuesday, September 2, 2025, Fairyland will celebrate all year with exciting special events for visitors of all ages. “Fairyland’s 75th anniversary celebrates the timeless magic of imagination, the boundless wonder of childhood, and the resilience of our community,” said Executive Director Kymberly Miller. “For generations, Fairyland has been an oasis where families escape the ordinary, craft cherished memories, and discover life’s simple joy of connection and belonging. As we honor 75 years of history and look to the next 75, we are committed to preserving Fairyland as a welcoming, joyful space where the spirit of imaginative play continues to shine.” To kick off its historic year Fairyland has unveiled a sparkling new lawn sign on Fairyland Hill overlooking Lake Merritt. The updated sign invites the community to join the yearlong festivities. Fairyland has planned a year filled with exciting events, new experiences, and collaborations to celebrate its 75th anniversary: park exploration and imaginative play and offers fun rewards yearround. 75th Anniversary Special Museum Feature: Opening Friday, April 4, 2025, a new collaborative installation titled “Fairyland @75: A Legacy of Magic” will be on view at the Oakland Museum of California (OMCA), highlighting Fairyland’s rich history, cultural impact, and enduring magic. New, Original Puppet Shows: Two brand-new productions will debut in 2025, adding to Fairyland’s renowned storytelling tradition. • What Makes a King (July 11– August 24): A story inspired by Maya myths that explores themes of leadership and courage. • Tío Conejo’s Big Wish (August 30–October 26): Fairyland’s first bilingual puppet show, based on a Cuban folktale about self-acceptance. Exclusive 75th Anniversary Merchandise: Including a limited-edition Magic Key (now on sale), Willie the Whale plushie (now on sale), and more to come. Fairyland’s Passport Card: Launching March 21, 2025, this in-park activity encourages 75th Birthday Party: On Labor Day, Monday, September 1, 2025Fairyland is hosting a Jubilee celebration featuring cakes from local bakeries, performances, arts & crafts activities, and other family-friendly activities—more details to come later in the year. Happily After Hours Events for Adults (21+): Fairyland’s four adult-only nights invite guests to experience the park after hours, without kids. Each themed evening features unique activities, entertainment, and the release of exclusive collectible prints created in collaboration with local artists. Full Calendar of Family Events: Explore every event happening throughout the year by visiting Fairyland’s Calendar of Events at https://fairyland.org/ assets/1672d2d183/FL.2025.CalendarofEvents.pdf. While the new sign celebrates this milestone year, Fairyland remains deeply committed to its collaboration with the Sogorea Te” Land Trust and its mission to honor the Ohlone people, the original stewards of this land. The “Children’s Ohloneland” sign, which first appeared in November 2024, will return later this year. In addition, Fairyland and Sogorea Te’ Land Trust are working on exciting future projects, including a puppet show debuting in 2026 that will highlight a story from the Ohlone culture.

articles.text: John and Sue Malick on a visit to Croatia. As residents of Piedmont for over 40 years, Sue and John Malick have demonstrated a love of the city rivaled only by their love for each other. John and Sue met on a blind date in 1972. Sue was an undergraduate at Wheaton College in Massachusetts studying political science and John had just started graduate school studying architecture at Yale. The couple dated for three years before getting married in 1975, two weeks after John finished his Masters degree. They married in Harvard, Massachusetts, a little town 30 miles west of Boston and unrelated to Harvard University. articles.text: Piedmont’s football team is back in the gym for their off-season weight lifting program led by assistant coaches Oski Tauaho (middle, left) and Bo Tauaho (middle, right). Early in the morning for the past four years a swarm of Piedmont High football players lines up at the school’s weight room to prepare for the season. Getting to Witter Field bright and early to lead the workouts are the offensive and defensive line coaches, Oski and Bo Tauaho. After winning two consecutive Western Alameda County Conference titles and the school’s first North Coast Section win since 2017, there’s no doubt about the success of the training program the Tauaho brothers have constructed. “We met head coach Seiden when he was running weights in the morning the season before we came on. We revamped how we lift weights; it’s just teaching them the mechanics behind it,” Oski said. “The results have been pretty good, just to see the development of the kids when they start with us. When we get toward the summer, you start to see the changes with them moving better and getting stronger,” mentioned Bo. Oski and Bo came to Piedmont High as members of coach Jordan Seiden’s staff in 2023, one year after his arrival when the school had to drop its varsity due to a small roster. Injuries were a major part of the 2022 team’s downfall, but after the arrival of Bo and Oski’s weight-lifting program, the number of injuries significantly dropped. “It’s been amazing to watch the football team grow. We came after the 2022 season and Jordan was telling us about the program. His plan was to just keeping it growing and we told him that we could run the weight-lifting; it’s a good way to get the kids out there. It’s not just playing football, you have to work out and have a good offseason too,” Bo said. “You lift weights in the offseason to prevent injuries when the season comes. You have to strengthen all of your muscles to prepared to rock and roll when the season comes,” Oski said. Since then, Piedmont won the 2023 WACC Shoreline title, receiving a berth in the D7 NCS playoffs. After a promotion to a more competitive division, they won the 2024 WACC Mission title and were undefeated against league opponents. With that, the sport’s popularity at the school has revived. It’s something that makes both coaches proud. “I’m proud of the guys. It starts with the players and if they lock in, they’ll see the results. Winning games starts in the offseason and the guys have been pretty good at committing to that. articles.text: Uncle Vanya, a heartbreaking comedy about the eternal battle between futility and change, opens at Berkeley Repertory Theatre February 14 through March 23. Olivier Award-winner Conor McPherson’s acclaimed adaptation of Anton Chekhov’s masterpiece will be directed by Shakespeare Theatre Company Artistic Director Simon Godwin, in a co-production with Berkeley Rep. Joining Golden Globe and Emmy Award nominee Hugh Bonneville as Vanya is Tony Award winner John Benjamin Hickey (Astrov), Ito Aghayere (Yelena), and Melanie Field (Sonya) When a distinguished elderly professor and owner of a rural estate returns home with a new young wife, Yelena, chaos erupts. Tensions run high, marriages reach their limits, as confessions and vodka flow freely. Two friends – Vanya, brother of the professor’s late first wife, who has long managed the estate, and Astrov, the local doctor – Golden Globe and Emmy Award nominee Hugh Bonneville plays the lead role as Vanya in a new adaptation of Chekhov’s haunting comedy Uncle Vanya at Berkeley Repertory Theatre, February 14 through March 23. both fall under Yelena’s spell while bemoaning the ennui of their provincial existence. Sonya, the professor’s daughter by his first wife, who has worked with Vanya to keep the estate going, suffers from her unrequited feelings for Astrov. articles.text: Opera San José Emeritus Artist-in-Residence Maria Natale sings the role of Judith and Zachary Nelson is Duke Bluebeard in a new production of Béla Bartók’s opera Bluebeard’s Castle Saturday through March 2. This Saturday, February 15 through March 2, Opera San José presents an all-new production of Béla Bartók’s chilling one-act opera Bluebeard’s Castle. This psychological thriller, directed by Opera San José (OSJ) General Director and CEO Shawna Lucey, follows Judith, a woman who uncovers terrifying corners of her new husband’s dark past while unlocking rooms in his eerie home. “Bluebeard’s Castle” will feature Emeritus OSJ Artist-in-Residence soprano Maria Natale — whose recent acclaimed portrayals at OSJ include the title role in Tosca and The Countess in The Marriage of Figaro — as the unwitting bride who comes to live in the haunted realm of a mysterious duke. Acclaimed baritone Zachary Nelson will make his OSJ debut as Duke Bluebeard, and OSJ Music Director Joseph Marcheso is set to conduct this powerful work. OSJ is collaborating with the Silicon Valley dance company New Ballet to feature three dancers as the previous wives of Duke Bluebeard: Delaney Ewert, Alysa Reinhardt and Sorcha Tate. The piece, including a libretto by Béla Balázs, will be performed in English, with both English and Spanish supertitles projected on stage. Bartók’s staggering opera premiered at the Royal Hungarian Opera House in Budapest in 1918. Based on, and departing from, the tale of Bluebeard from French folklore, the opera delves into psychological themes of love, trust and the unknowable depths of the human soul. The work is acclaimed for its lush and evocative orchestration, which conveys the dark, mysterious atmosphere of Bluebeard’s castle, and its dramatic vocal writing for the two characters, Bluebeard and Judith. Bartók’s innovative use of Hungarian folk music influences and modernist techniques creates a gripping narrative soundscape and has remained a cornerstone of 20th century opera, praised for its emotional intensity and symbolic depth. “I can’t wait to bring this mesmerizing opera to our audiences,” said Lucey. “Besides its stunning orchestration, the work is emotional and unforgettable. From fierce brass sections to rich strings and sonorous woodwinds, the music and terrifically challenging vocals take us on a truly chilling thrill ride for a little over an hour. Fasten your seat belts for this memorable one-act work.” “Classically Curious” night for Bluebeard’s Castle will be held Friday, February 21, bringing together people who have a passion for deepening their involvement with opera. This program was created to introduce new audiences to opera, offering access to discounted tickets, exclusive behind-the-scenes opportunities and social events that connect emerging opera lovers. More information can be found at go.operasj.org/ClassicallyCurious. To buy tickets ($58–$215) for the performance at California Theatre (345 S 1st St., San Jose), visit operasj.org, or call the box office at 408-437-4450.

articles.text: Smuin Contemporary Ballet will present its Choreography Showcase in San Francisco, this Friday through February 23. Ten premieres will be unveiled ranging from humorous to heartfelt and featuring a variety of dance styles and musical selections. Presented at the Smuin Center for Dance, these intimate performances will provide audiences with an invaluable glimpse at the rising choreographic voices within the company. Smuin will also host preshow talks and post-show Q&As, in which audiences will enjoy insights into the program and creative process behind the ballets. This thrilling opportunity for audiences to experience never-before-seen world premieres by first-time and rising dancemakers was inspired by founder Michael Smuin’s commitment to put the artistic reins into the hands of dancers, providing them with the time, space and talent to develop their choreographic skills. “Choreography is a honed skill that takes practice, mentorship, and training,” said Smuin Artistic Director Amy Seiwert, a nationally acclaimed choreographer, as well as a former dancer. “Creating dance requires resources that aren’t always easy to access, such as skilled dancers and a dedicated space. Opportunities are rare in the ballet field but are so important in fostering the next generation of creative leaders.” Smuin Director Emerita Celia Fushille formalized the tradition by launching the company’s firstever Choreography Showcase in 2008. Since then, the opportunity has repeated annually or once every two years, with several of the works developed in the Showcase process adapted for mainstage premieres at Smuin. Experiences such as these are uncommon, particularly in the field of ballet, as they are logistically and financially difficult to organize. “We are investing in our dancers to become stronger collaborators,” added Seiwert. “The experience is incredibly valuable as they gain an understanding of what it takes to create a piece, and strengthens their skill set as a dancer working on premieres by other creators.” Tickets ($35-$55) and schedule information for the shows at Smuin Center for Dance (1830 17th Street, San Francisco) are available online at smuinballet. org, or by phone at 415-912-1899. articles.text: Works of women composers to be performed livestreamed The Shoreline Piano Trio presents “Exploration of Love and Art,” a concert celebrating the works of women composers this Valentine’s Day, Friday at 8 p.m., at Old First Presbyterian Church in San Francisco. The concert will also be livestreamed by the trio – violinist Sui-mi Shin, cellist Katie Youn and pianist Menghua Lin. The program includes works by Caroline Shaw, Maria Theresia von Paradis, Jessie Montgomery, Amy Beach, Pulitzer Prize-winner Jennifer Higdon, and the iconic Romantic composer Clara Schumann. Sue-mi Shin is an avid chamber violinist, orchestral performer and music educator. She was one of the founding members of Yule Piano Trio and Sonnet Ensemble, where she served as the artistic director for many seasons. As an active orchestral performer, she plays with the Opera San Jose orchestra, Symphony San Jose and Monterey Symphony among many others. She holds degrees from Manhattan School of Music and Yale University. Katie Youn has appeared as a cellist in concerts throughout North America, South America, Europe and Asia, in venues including Boston’s Symphony Hall and Jordan Hall, Japan’s Suntory and Minatomirai Hall, Vancouver’s Orpheum Hall, and Vatican City’s St. Peter’s Basilica. She regularly appears with Sound Impact, Chamber Music Silicon Valley, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra and Sonnet Ensemble. She holds Bachelor and Master of Music degrees from the New England Conservatory and a Doctorate of Musical Arts form Boston University. Menghua Lin began her piano studies at four, winning prestigious competitions including the Pittsburgh Concert Society, Steinway Society West Pennsylvania, Chautauqua Music Festival Concerto Competition and YAMAHA Piano Competition. She holds a degrees in piano performance from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Carnegie Mellon University and the Manhattan School of Music. articles.text: Immersive science and art exhibition runs Feb. 15 through April 27 This Saturday through April 27, experience our solar system like never before at the breathtaking exhibition “Look Up: Eclipse, Moon, and Mars,” at the Exploratorium in San Francisco. Feel the thrill of space exploration as you immerse yourself in the beauty of a total solar eclipse, marvel at monumental realistic sculptures of the Moon and Mars and explore the rovers supporting NASA’s latest breakthroughs in space exploration. This cosmic experience will spark curiosities of all ages and inspire your imagination of our solar system and humanity’s next great frontier — space “‘Look Up’ brings the excitement of space exploration to life through art, science and technology,” said Rob Semper, chief science officer at the Exploratorium. “This exhibition is a rare opportunity to explore the tools and results of our ongoing exploration of the solar system’s most breathtaking phenomena, right here on Earth.” “Perfect for explorers of all ages, ‘Look Up’ is more than just a visit – it’s an invitation to discover, share, and be inspired,” said Sylvia Algire, Director of Museum Experience. Exhibition highlights include: Immersive eclipse experience Step into the awe-inspiring phenomenon of a total solar eclipse. Produced in collaboration with Montreal-based multimedia production studio Supply + Demand, this prototype experience uses state-of-the-art visuals and soundscapes to capture the magic of this celestial event. The Moon and Mars Marvel at breathtaking largescale planetary sculptures by British installation artist Luke Jerram. His featured work, “Museum of the Moon and Mars,” is inspired by Jerram’s childhood in Bristol, UK, where the moon-tugged tides are the second-highest in the world. This artwork, printed from 120 dpi NASA imagery, shows the moon’s every cliff and crater at an approximate scale of 1:700,000; one inch of the sculpture equals about 11 miles of the lunar surface. NASA’s Mars Rovers and Orbiters Meet NASA space explorers Perseverance, Sojourner, Odyssey and more, and discover how these groundbreaking missions are helping us learn about Mars, the Red Planet. These remarkable instruments are on display thanks to a special loan from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The exhibition also builds on the Exploratorium’s decades-long partnership with NASA to livestream total solar eclipses from across the globe, making this a uniquely rich and immersive experience for visitors. The Exploratorium (Pier 15 Embarcadero at, Green St, San Francisco) is open 10 a.m. through 5 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday (with additional Exploratorium After Dark hours from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m. on Thursday), and 12 p.m. through 5 p.m. on Sunday For more information and to purchase tickets ($39.95 for adults 18-64, $29.95 for youth 4-7, teachers, students and seniors), please visit exploratorium.edu/ space or call 415-528-4444. articles.text: Production delights audience and dancers Tamara Rojo’s inaugurated her third season as Artistic Director of the San Francisco Ballet with Sir Kenneth MacMillan’s Manon, an evocative ballet about the dangers of desire. Set in pre-revolutionary France, the ballet charts the transformation of Manon from a naïve girl on her way to join a convent to a passionate lover, courtesan, and ultimately a prisoner transported from Paris to New Orleans, offering an exploration of the challenges faced by a woman in a society constrained by class and wealth. Far from a fairy tale, this is a story of passion and despair, portrayed through profoundly expressive choreography. Despite the demanding nature of their roles, the dancers clearly reveled in performances, their enthusiasm matched by those of the audience. MacMillan, of Scottish descent, transformed British ballet, steering it away from the refined lyricism of Fredrich Ashton and the structured classicism of Ninette de Valois, his predecessors at the Royal Opera House. Known as the “angry young man” of dance—akin to John Osborne in literature— MacMillan is celebrated for ushering The Royal Ballet into an era of psychological realism and intense emotional storytelling. Manon, which debuted at the Royal Opera House in London in 1974, showcases a fusion of modern dance shapes with classical ballet lines. The ballet moves at a fast cinematic pace, transitioning between continents and times periods, yet always firmly rooted in the characters’ psychological reality. On January 31st, the last evening performance of the season, the title role of Manon was danced by Nikisha Fogo, the Company’s first black female principal dancer—and a new tour de force whose athleticism and technical brilliance is magnified by her radiant onstage presence. Aaron Robison danced the role of Des Grieux, a young student who falls in love with the beautiful Manon. Their on-stage chemistry was palpable, adding a layer of complexity to an otherwise standard naïve young lovers’ conceit. They were brilliantly paired with Fernando Carratalá Coloma as Manon’s brother Lescaut and Katherine Barkman as his mistress. All four dancers transcended typical ballet character archetypes, emerging as fully realized individuals while demonstrating remarkable command of their discipline. Two scenes were particularly striking. First, the drunken dance in Act 2, where Lescaut, portrayed by Coloma, must navigate a lavish party while inebriated. MacMillan’s choreography brilliantly captures his intoxication as an artistic feat—his movements are unpredictably off-kilter; his legs buckle, he lunges as if gravity betrays him, and he collapses into his mistress’s arms, only to be jerked upright again. This pas de deux strikes a precarious balance between humor and menace, showcasing Coloma’s impressive technical and artistic skills. Second, the more sinister scene in Act 3 features Manon being assaulted by a Louisiana prison guard. Earlier tender moments between Manon and her lover give way to the brutal force of a man who views her as merely an object. Fogo’s portrayal of Manon in this scene is harrowing—she flails and convulses, sometimes from almost impossible positions, like lifting her legs nearly 90 degrees while lying face down. Her frantic, desperate resistance leads to heavy, uncontrolled falls that deviate from classical ballet’s grace, underlining the realism of her terror and accentuating her vulnerability. The compelling dancing is complemented by dynamic, sumptuous sets and exquisite costumes. Both evoke scenes of extreme poverty and decadent wealth—the two worlds between which the characters oscillate. Lavish gowns crafted from lace and tulle dazzle the eye, set in stark contrast to the ragged clothing of the poor. San Francisco’s performances of Manon revive the iconic 1974 sets and costumes Photo by Lindsay Thomas Jasmine Jimison in Manon originally created for the Royal Ballet by the renowned designer Nicholas Georgiadis. Within the costume waistbands, one can find the names of all the cast members who have worn them since 1974. “It is an incredible honor when you get to wear a costume that perhaps was once on the stage, on the body of an artist you admire,” Rojo remarked. Among those names on the bands was Rojo’s own, as she has also danced the lead role in Manon. The seemingly effortless beauty and elegance of the San Francisco Ballet’s Manon, which belies the long weeks of strenuous rehearsals, costume fittings, and set management, was not lost on the audience. The theater was packed, and the applause at the end was longer than usual. Manon represents a strong start to the 2025 season for the San Francisco Ballet and is yet another gift to the city from this renowned company. It is especially valuable at a time when beauty and enjoyment are hard to come by. Anastasia Edel is an American writer and arts critic for the Piedmont Post. articles.text: Don’t miss an artful weekend with the California Watercolor Association’s 55th International Exhibition this Saturday. Return on Sunday to the Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) for Music by In the Tradition jazz trio. Watercolor exhibition Join the California Watercolor Association (CWA) in celebrating the 85 artists selected by juror Michael Holter for this year’s international exhibition on February 15, 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. at PCA. The awards, totaling an estimated $16,000 in cash and sponsorships, will honor the top 20 paintings selected by Awards Juror, artist Gary Bukovnik. CWA’s free annual event, honoring exceptional watermedia paintings from talented artists worldwide, will be running from Saturday through March 23. It will continue to be free from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays, and will also be viewable for attendees of other events at PCA. Organized in 1967 as East Bay Watercolor Society, it changed its name in 1996. Throughout the decades, the organization has continued to support artists and students working in watermedia through community outreach programs, workshops, public exhibitions, scholarships and student workshops. Don’t miss this opportunity to see this exhibition of some of the world’s finest new watercolor works. No tickets are necessary. In the Tradition Join Bill Jackman, Albert Brooks and Michael Jones in celebrating Valentine’s Day with “In the Spirit of Love!” at PCA on February 16 at 4:30 p.m. This skilled jazz piano trio will play all your favorite love songs from the 1910s through the 1960s including ballads, swing, a little Latin flavor and even some blues — sweetened by complimentary refreshments. This Sunday’s lineup of jazz and pop standards includes “You Made Me Love You” (1913), “Someone to Watch Over Me” (1926), “I Only Have Eyes for You” (1934), “I’m in the Mood for Love” (1935), “Like Someone in Love” (1944), “That’s Amore” (1952), “Never on Sunday” (1960) and many more. Bill Jackman, playing with the trio for the past 30 years, was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher, who for several decades presided over the grand piano at the former Solomon Grundy’s (now Skates) on the Berkeley Marina. Jackman is also a Lupita Records musician who has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Michael Jones is a bassist and band leader who has played throughout the Bay Area for over 30 years. After studying music at the University of Northern Colorado, he moved to the Bay Area in the mid-1970s, where he played with many icons including Al Tanner, Faye Carroll, Ed Kelley, Donald Bailey, Pharoah Sanders and Buddy Montgomery. As a sideman and bandleader, Jones has served as the music director for the Golden Gate Library Summer Concert and Jam Session series in Oakland for the past 23 years. Albert Brooks grew up dancing to Latin music in the South Bronx, playing these rhythms on any percussion instrument he could get his hands on. Alongside Latin drumming, he added trap drums to his musical offerings several decades ago and fluently melds these with swing rhythms. He has juggled his growth as a drummer with the demands of being a practicing obstetrician-gynecologist in the East Bay for nearly 30 years, having graduated in 1974 from the Albert Einstein College of Medicine of Yeshiva University in New York City. $25 advance tickets are available at piedmontcenterforthearts. org, or $30 at the door by cash or check. articles.text: Bounce opens in a Chicago airport, the weather heavy snow, flights are delayed or cancelled. Three waiting passengers are gathered around a small table near a crowded bar. Strangers, they exchange names and professions: Mimi (Natasha Henstridge). Buddy (Ben Affleck), and Greg (Tony Goldwyn). Mimi is on her way to Dallas, Buddy and Greg are waiting for their L.A. flights to open up. Greg learns that his flight was just cancelled, and he shows them his gifted hotel voucher. Mimi and Buddy are still hopeful their flights, though pushed, will depart. Buddy has been told that his flight will be the last to L.A. They are three personable, attractive and eager to get home. Greg shares that he is married with two young boys (it is the holidays and he has promised his wife, Abby (Gwyneth Paltrow), that he will hurry back to take them Christmas tree shopping). Gwyneth Paltrow and Ben Affleck in Bounce All of the above is just a brief introduction to the next two acts that follow. To say more would deprive the audience of a story that becomes incrementally compelling. It’s enough to say that with each scene the question is asked: will Buddy seize the moment? Of course he doesn’t. Bounce brings to mind the Sydney Pollack film Random Hearts, also layered with multiple questions that are only partially resolved. It stars Harrison Ford and Kristen Scott Thomas as two strangers who share a devastating tragedy that changes their lives forever. Now Streaming on apple tv/prime/Fandango. Bounce. articles.text: Talent and musical genius often runs in the family. Johann Sebastian Bach had 20 musical children and a very large and talented extended family. We remember Frederick the Great for his military genius. Perhaps we need to remember him for his musical genius. And believe it or not, his two sisters were equally Other famous musical families include the brother and sister duo of Felix and Danny Mendelssohn, and three generations of Mozarts. In our area we are happy to mention the Menuhin family with a brother and two sisters, and the Ricci family with two brothers More recently, the Hansen family has been active on the music scene. The father was a noted band conductor, and son Eric Hansen has been the subject of this column on many occasions. He continues as the brilliant conductor of the Prometheus Eric‘s younger sister Robin Hansen is a noted violinist in our area. As such, she is a stalwart performer in many orchestras. For her concert yesterday afternoon in the Berkeley City Club she gathered some important musicians for a chamber music concert. Joining her were pianist John Wilson, violinist Ani Bukujian, violinist Elizabeth Prior, and cellist Saul Richmond-Rakerd. The program itself was out of the ordinary. It began with a Piano Trio by Amy Beach, then a String Quartet by Mozart, and finished off with a Piano Quintet by Samuel Coleridge-Taylor. The musical proficiency of the performers was obvious from the very beginning. I was particularly interested in the tone that Robin Hansen draws from her violin. Lombardi A cable car ride to the country was the perfect way to spend a Sunday afternoon in the 1890s. From 1890 to 1893, riding the cable car to the Piedmont hills was a favorite pastime. Cable cars provided convenient transportation for residents in the Piedmont hills to downtown Oakland and San Francisco, and almost more importantly, they brought visitors and future residents into the hills. In 1873, Andrew Hallidie built the first cable car line in San Francisco, and by 1889, there were eight cable car lines in the city. The first cable car in Oakland was running in 1886 along San Pablo Avenue. “8,000 passengers rode the cable cars [into Piedmont on the opening day of the cable car company in 1890].” A cable car stops at the passenger shelter at Oakland and Vernal Avenues before turning north on the turntable towards Blair Park. Note the vacant In 1890, the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company began operating a cable car line into the Piedmont hills. The company built a large brick powerhouse to run two cables. One cable ran from the powerhouse up Oakland Avenue to Vernal Avenue (now Highland). The other cable ran to 8th and Clay Streets in downtown Oakland. Steam from the powerful engines heated the water for the popular Piedmont Baths next door. The opening day for the cable car to Piedmont was August 1, 1890. The cable company reported that 8,000 passengers rode their cable cars that day. While some cars were open, new green cable cars were designed with large windows and roofs “six to eight inches higher than those of other cars, so as to give passengers a better view of the scenery on route.” This was quite an improvement from the old horse cars. The Consolidated Piedmont Cable Car Company ran five cable cars on Oakland Avenue every day and seven cars on Sunday. The tracks were set in solid concrete with a trench for the cable. To encourage more riders, the cable car company leased Blair Park and added many attractions including a bandstand for concerts on Saturdays and Sundays. Later, balloon ascensions with daring aerialists drew visitors to the park by cable car. These attractions also were expensive, and the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Car Company failed to make a profit each year it ran. Though the cable car company did not prosper, it was a boon to early Piedmont real estate. Cable cars brought efficient public transportation to Piedmont. Many weekend visitors enjoyed the views and the climate and decided to build their homes here. A good number of Piedmont’s early 20th century houses were built near the cable car line on Oakland Avenue. It’s not surprising that the early horse cars, cable cars and electric streetcars were built by real estate investors. articles.text: The previous two Wednesdays the Walking on Wednesdays group had visited projects that the Piedmont Beautification Foundation has supported over its 60 years of serving Piedmont. There was a strong turnout of 56 walkers and five K-9 best friends forth e final tour of PBF projects. The morning started at the Exedra with PBF President Patty Dunlap providing an overview of PBF’s history and what the walkers were going to see. At each location a PBF volunteer would tell them about the project’s history and PBF’s contribution. The first contributions, the Exedra Blue Vase, Exedra Plaza, and McGee Overlook, were right in front of them. Patty shared that this site was originally the location of the Piedmont Springs Hotel that Walter Blair built in 1871. After the hotel burned down in 1892, Frank C. Havens developed his Piedmont Park, a park café, a Japanese Tea House, and other attractions. After Havens died in 1918, the City purchased most of the park and hired Albert Farr in 1922 to design a City Center Master Plan. The Exedra and Community Hall were part of it and were dedicated in 1925. PBF’s first Exedra renovation began in 1972 with Blue Vase Triangle plantings, major structural and decorative repairs, iron gates, and lighting. In 2000, PBF also made major donations to the development of the Exedra Plaza, which is at the backside of the vase. The McGee Overlook was added with the Centennial Oak Grove. The Plaza was a great background for a group photo. The group then went across the top of the park to the Tea House where Cameron Wolfe and former Piedmont mayor and PBF president Valerie Matzger were waiting for them. Valerie and Cameron said this is not the original tea house that Havens built in 1907 as an attraction for his Piedmont Park. When the City acquired the land in the 1920s, the original tea house and many other park features were torn down to make room for the new Civic Center. In 1976 the Leander Redmon estate at Hillside and Magnolia Avenues was razed to build the new Piedmont Middle School. The estate had a tea house that was donated to the city and moved on a flatbed truck to its current site on a Sunday morning with many citizens watching. Next, the walkers went to the top of the park and the Highland-Guilford Steps where Gayle Lambert was there to tell them about this project. On a rainy winter day before Covid, she and Ruthie McCloud were walking down this path and found the railroad tie stairs uneven and slippery with no handrails. They met Chester Nakahara, the public works director, and Nancy Kent, the parks and project manager, and a renovation project was developed. The group then went across the top of the park to the Tea House where Cameron Wolfe and former Piedmont mayor and PBF president Valerie Matzger were waiting for them. Valerie and Cameron said this is not the original tea house that Havens built in 1907 as an attraction for his Piedmont Park. When the City acquired the land in the 1920s, the original tea house and many other park features were torn down to make room for the new Civic Center. In 1976 the Leander Redmon estate at Hillside and Magnolia Avenues was razed to build the new Piedmont Middle School. The estate had a tea house that was donated to the city and moved on a flatbed truck to its current site on a Sunday morning with many citizens watching. Next, the walkers went to the top of the park and the Highland-Guilford Steps where Gayle Lambert was there to tell them about this project. On a rainy winter day before Covid, she and Ruthie McCloud were walking down this path and found the railroad tie stairs uneven and slippery with no handrails. They met Chester Nakahara, the public works director, and Nancy Kent, the parks and project manager, and a renovation project was developed. It was approved by the City Council in 2021 with $55,000 from PBF and the Piedmont Garden Club and $100,000 from the City. The wooden steps were replaced with colored concrete, landings, metal handrails, landscaping, six benches, and a small plaza. The walkers continued to Sheridan and Wildwood Avenues and up to the Hall Fenway, a scenic path that connects Wildwood and Crocker Avenues. Down the path was Sharon Hom ready to share more PBF history. This area once served as the right-of-way for the early 20th Century Key System’s #10 line streetcar, which ran through Piedmont until 1948. When the line was terminated, much of the right-of-way was sold for infill home developments. AC Transit even briefly used the land to park buses. However, Herbert Edwin Hall, a nearby King Avenue resident, convinced the City to obtain the property and he worked with neighbors to raise funds to acquire it in 1963. When PBF was established in 1964, it adopted the Fenway as one of its first major projects and raised more funds to complete its transformation. To honor Herbert Hall’s pivotal role, the path was officially named “Hall Fenway.” To ensure its long-term beauty, PBF has contributed $4,000 annually for plant maintenance. She explained that this sculpture was the work of internationally renowned sculptor, Benny Bufano, and was a gift from Jerry S. Mosher to the citizens of Piedmont. Its placement in the park followed four years of negotiations between the PBF, the Piedmont City Council, and the Bufano Society of the Arts. This acquisition, valued at between $40,000 and $50,000 at the time, was installed in 1980 by Rigging International, a company owned by Piedmont resident Denny McLeod. It is number nine in a limited addition of 25 Bufano sculptures and is composed of polished ground granite that weighs 2 1/2 tons. PBF, led by then President Norma Wells, raised $4,700 to help with installation and landscaping. The bears were restored and cleaned in 2000, and a wrought iron bench was renovated in 2009. articles.text: On February 11, 1980, Benny Bufano’s iconic sculpture, Nursing Bear and Cubs, found its permanent home in Crocker Park. The successful installation was made possible through the generosity of Denny McLeod and his company, Rigging International, after a three-year campaign by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. Nursing Bear and Cubs is Number 9 of a limited edition of 25 sculptures, with only five pieces thought to be in the Bay Area. The sculpture is made of ground granite, stands over five feet tall, and weighs 2.5 tons. At the time of its arrival, its estimated value was $40,000. About Beniamino Bufano Beniamino Bufano, the creator of “The Bears,” as we often refer to the sculpture, was born in Italy in 1890. He moved to the United States with his family in 1910, first settling in New York City, and then relocating to San Francisco in 1915. Bufano’s first public commission in San Francisco was for the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in 1915, where he created a piece for the Court of the Universe on the Arch of Triumph. In his early years, Bufano became known for his sculptures with themes of peace and, in later years, animal-themed works like the Nursing Bear and Cubs. His art can still be seen in various public places in San Francisco. Bufano died in August of 1970, more than ten years before Nursing Bear and Cubs was installed in Crocker Park. The gift and community effort The sculpture was a gift from Jerry S. Mosher, a longtime collector of Bufano’s works and principal owner of Mosher Investment Services, based in Lafayette. As an Oakland resident and Piedmont neighbor, Mosher hoped that the community would appreciate the sculpture and that he would be able to enjoy it as well. Upon hearing about Mosher’s offer of the sculpture, Norma Wells, who was President of PBF at the time, was keen to make the project a reality. She enlisted Jean Wolfe, with whom she had previously worked on the Tea House project in Piedmont Park. They contacted Bob Leefeldt, a former Chair of the Park Commission and a long-time champion of Crocker Park, to join the cause. However, the timing was difficult. Proposition 13 had just passed, and local governments throughout California were thrown into financial chaos. Piedmont, like many cities, was struggling with budget constraints, and there were concerns about how to fund the sculpture’s acquisition and maintenance. Some were skeptical of PBF’s ability to raise the required funds. The project was also met with debates about where the sculpture should be placed. Despite the challenges, Wells, Wolfe, Leefeldt, and other PBF trustees worked tirelessly over three years and eventually secured the necessary funds on behalf of PBF. These funds spared the City unwanted expenses and provided the crucial support needed. After a contentious City Council meeting, the decision to proceed with the acquisition was narrowly approved by a 3-to-2 vote, and the project moved forward. sculpture was installed, and a grand celebration followed. The Piedmonter newspaper shared a heartwarming moment from the event. A young girl said, “I hope no one ever hurts it.” She is not named in the article, but this author has a suspicion. Lilla Wells, then 8 years old, attended the celebration with her grandmother Norma Wells who was presiding. Lilla, the daughter of former Mayor Susan Hill, and now an adult living in Piedmont, recently said she “is proud that many residents now call it ‘Bear Park’ rather than Crocker Park. Walk through the park on any given day and you will see small children playing around and on the Bears. It is a happy ending to an “only in Piedmont” story.
